comments.content: Priority is inverted: the setting-derived path is unshifted first, then the PATH-derived path is unshifted *on top of it*. So when both succeed, `which pi` wins — exactly the opposite of the "highest priority" comment. A user who explicitly sets `pi-agent.binaryPath` to a specific install (e.g. a pinned SDK) will silently get a different SDK from PATH. (The `PI_HOME`/`PI_AGENT_DIR` unshift blocks further below outrank both, which also contradicts the comment.)

None of the candidate-probing code is wrapped in try/catch, so an `fs` throw (EACCES on a shared install dir, ELOOP on a cyclic symlink, ENOTDIR/ENOENT on a `readdirSync` of a non-directory) escapes `findPiSdkAtPath()` and the `for (const piNodeModules of possiblePaths)` loop, aborting the whole `load()` call at require time with a raw stack trace instead of the friendly "PI CLI not installed" stub — and losing the graceful degradation the rest of the function implements. The same unguarded pattern exists in the two pnpm version-dir scans and the mise `installs/` category walk. Wrap the body of `load()` (or at least each probe) so a broken candidate only skips that candidate; the stale `attemptedPaths` list is already collected for the error message.

The double-hook guard keeps the *first* hook installed, so `piNodeModules` is captured in that hook's closure forever. If the extension is reloaded (Developer: Restart Extension Host, window reload after installing/updating PI) and a different install is discovered, the stale path stays in effect and the newly found one is ignored — `hookModuleResolution(piNodeModules)` silently becomes a no-op. Store the SDK root on the function object so a re-hook can refresh it instead of pinning the first result.

A directory without an `index.js` is returned as-is. `Module._resolveFilename` results are consumed by `Module._load`, which will treat the extensionless path as `.js` and try to read the directory as a file, producing a confusing `EISDIR` instead of a clean resolution failure. Return `null` so the caller falls through to Node's normal resolution/error.

The traversal check is purely lexical on the *logical* path. PI installs are pnpm/mise symlink farms, so a symlink placed inside the package directory resolves outside it and this check passes — the hook then hands that path to `Module._load` and executes it. Validate the real path of the target (when it exists) against the real path of `pkgDir` before returning it.

`which/where pi`, `npm root -g` and `pnpm root -g` are blocking `spawnSync` calls on the extension host's single thread, each with a 3s timeout — up to ~9s of a frozen extension host before any extension code runs, and they execute even when the SDK was already located via the setting or the `pi` binary (because the candidate list is fully built before the search loop). These two probes should be lazy: only run them if the cheap filesystem candidates fail.

This is a near-verbatim copy of the pnpm scan ~45 lines above (including the unguarded `fs.readdirSync(versionedPath)`, which can throw on a permission-denied pnpm dir and break activation). Extract one helper and call it for both bases so a layout change only has to be made once.

This `statSync` sits *outside* the per-category try/catch, so a single broken symlink or unreadable entry under `installs/` (e.g. `pi-coding-agent-old` → deleted target) throws and aborts the whole mise scan, silently skipping every remaining category. The inner `catch` comment says "try next category", which only holds for errors raised inside the inner loop.

comments.content: The header documents a dependency on Node 22+'s `require(esm)`, but `package.json` declares `engines.vscode: ^1.85.0` (Electron 25 → Node 18). On any VS Code older than the one shipping Node ≥22.12 this require throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` and the user only sees the generic "PiLot Studio failed to load" message with no indication of the Node version. Either raise `engines.vscode`, or detect the capability up front (e.g. `process.features.require_module` / Node major version) and surface an actionable error.
Floating promise: `showErrorMessage(...).then(...)` has no rejection handler, so a rejected promise (e.g. the host shutting down) becomes an unhandled rejection. Prefer async/await with a try/catch.

Every intercepted `require("@earendil-works/...")` re-reads and re-parses the package's `package.json` synchronously, and each sub-path import re-runs 1–2 `existsSync` calls. The results never change for the lifetime of the process — memoize them in a `Map` keyed by package directory.

Hard-coded five-level `..` walk-up is fragile: it silently breaks if the pnpm store layout shifts by one level, and it is inconsistent with the `lastIndexOf("/node_modules/")` strategy used a few lines above specifically to handle nested node_modules. Reuse `extractNodeModulesPath()` on a plausible `dist/cli.js` path under `linkTarget` instead.

The palette is hard-coded dark, but `color-scheme` is never declared. Without `color-scheme: dark` the UA treats the document as a light page, so form-widget internals, `<select>` popup, `input[type=search]` clear affordance, the document scrollbar gutter and the default `::placeholder` color are all rendered with light-mode defaults against a `#09090b` surface (e.g. a light `<select>` dropdown, and a placeholder gray whose contrast against the near-black `--input-bg` drops below 4.5:1). Declaring the color scheme once at the token root fixes the whole class of issues.

This brutalist state is encoded with `background` fill + hard `box-shadow` + `transform`. In Windows High Contrast (`forced-colors: active`) the UA forces author backgrounds and drops box-shadows entirely, so the button's only boundary (its `border: 1px solid var(--color-border)`, itself ~1.7:1) and both hover/active cues disappear. Add a `forced-colors` block that re-establishes boundaries and state using system colors, and raise border contrast in `prefers-contrast: more`.

Focus indication is only defined for native `button`/`input`/`textarea`/`select`. The app also ships non-form keyboard widgets — e.g. `div.session-panel[role="listbox"][tabindex="0"]` (SessionTree.svelte:183-190), `div[role="button"][tabindex="0"]` (Header/ModelSelector/SkillsPanel), and `tabindex="0"` scroll regions (ChatPanel:951, MessageBubble:980). Those elements fall back to the UA default ring only, and any scoped rule that sets `outline: none` (e.g. `.session-panel { outline: none }`, SessionTree.svelte:381) leaves them with **no visible focus indicator at all** — a WCAG 2.4.7 failure for the session tree, which is fully keyboard-driven. Provide a global baseline for ARIA-widget / tabindex targets. Note that `:where(...)` (0 specificity) will *not* beat a scoped `.class` rule, so the outline must be `!important` (or the components must be fixed) to be effective here.

The comment above this block claims a real outline "survives scoped component styles" — that is not true for the failure mode that actually exists in the codebase: scoped rules that set `outline: none` with *higher* specificity than `input:focus` (0,1,1) simply win. Example: ChatPanel.svelte:1742-1750 uses `.messages :global(.search-input) { outline: none; }` (0,2,0), which overrides this declaration, so the message-search input has zero focus feedback. Either forbid `outline: none` in scoped styles, or make this rule win.

`--color-border` / `--color-divider` are both `#3f3f46`, which is ~1.9:1 against `--color-bg` and ~1.7:1 against `--color-surface`. That is fine as a decorative divider, but it is also the only boundary for the default `button` (`border: 1px solid var(--color-border)`) and for `::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb`, where WCAG 1.4.11 requires 3:1 for a UI component boundary — the scrollbar thumb will be near-invisible on the `#09090b` track. Introduce a dedicated higher-contrast token for interactive/scrollbar boundaries.

comments.content: This blanket `input` selector also matches `checkbox`, `radio`, `range`, `color`, `file` and `search` inputs, which today only survive because components happen to hide them (`opacity: 0; width: 0; height: 0` in `.toggle input`). Any visible native control will pick up a 2px border, 12px/16px padding and the monospace font, producing an oversized, misaligned control. Scope the rule to text-like inputs.

The press effect moves the button down/right by 2px. Because `html, body { overflow: hidden }`, a button flush against the right/bottom edge of the shell is clipped by those 2px on :active (and its 1px border + shadow can be cut). Same for the reverse on the hover lift when a button sits against a `overflow: hidden` panel. Express press feedback with the box-shadow only, or keep the transform but ensure the shell reserves the offset.

`#app` is a flex column whose children default to `min-height: auto`, so a panel that forgets its own `overflow` (the exact scenario the comment on `html, body` warns about) cannot shrink: it grows past the shell and the surplus is silently clipped and unreachable. Setting `min-height: 0` on direct children makes the per-region overflow contract actually hold rather than depending on every component remembering it.

The reduced-motion override only cancels `transition` on four element selectors and `transform` on the same set. Everything else — `@keyframes` animations, `animation` shorthand, `scroll-behavior` declared in components — keeps running, and the invariant that "component styles handle their own media queries" is not enforceable from this file. A single global safety net makes the preference hold app-wide without auditing every component.

This comment asserts a renderer-side mitigation that does not exist. I searched all of `src/webview/` for `on:error`, `onerror`, and error listeners: the only hit is `reader.onerror` in `ChatPanel.svelte:855` (a `FileReader` error), and no `` element in `MessageBubble.svelte:866`, `:997` or `ChatPanel.svelte:1052,1129,1303` has an error handler. So when CSP correctly blocks an image (the very outcome this policy is designed to produce), the user sees a broken-image icon with no diagnostic and no placeholder. The other half of the claim ("data: URIs are unbounded — cap accepted size/content-type") is likewise unenforced on the inbound path: `ChatPanel.svelte:830` caps only *locally pasted* files (`MAX_IMAGE_BYTES`/`MAX_IMAGES`), while images arriving from the host go through `getImageDataUrl(img)` in `MessageBubble.svelte:865-867` with no size or MIME check. Since this file is the authoritative place the CSP contract is documented, either (a) implement the caps in the renderer so the comment becomes true, or (b) reword it to state the current unmitigated state and link the tracking issue. Leaving a comment that describes a control that was never built is worse than documenting the gap.

comments.content:
The host-side rewrite is regex-based and silently no-ops on a mismatch. `getWebviewContent()` in `src/pi-agent-provider.ts` uses:

- `/(<meta[^>]*http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"[^>]*content=")([^"]*)("[^>]*>)/i` — requires `http-equiv` to appear *before* `content` in the tag.
- `policy.replaceAll("'self'", ...)` — requires the literal token `'self'` with single quotes.
- `policy.replace(/script-src([^;]*);/, ...)` — injects the nonce into the *first* `script-src` occurrence, so the directive must remain a single statement terminated by `;`.

If a future edit reorders the attributes, switches the quote style, or reformats the policy across multiple `content` attributes, every one of these replacements fails quietly. The result is a shipped webview with `script-src 'self'` and no `cspSource`: the media-globals script is blocked, `window.__MEDIA_ICON__`/`__MEDIA_KOFI__` are `undefined`, and there is no error — just missing icons. The failure mode is a silent security/functionality downgrade, which is the most expensive kind.

This is partly guarded by `src/test/suite/realhost-webview-csp.test.ts`, but only for the *built* `dist/webview/index.html`; a stale build makes the suite throw a setup error rather than pinpoint the source of the format change. Since the header comment already declares this tag authoritative, please record the format constraints inline so a maintainer reformatting the HTML knows the exact token shape that must be preserved.

comments.content: The exported config object is completely untyped. Because this is a plain `.js` module in a `"type": "module"` project and `svelte-check` is run with `tsconfig.webview.json` (which does not type-check this file), any typo or unsupported key inside `compilerOptions`/`preprocess` is accepted silently and only surfaces as a confusing compile-time error deep in the build. Svelte 5 exports a `Config` type for exactly this file — add a JSDoc annotation (or convert to `svelte.config.ts`) so the config is validated at edit time.

comments.content: Glob key omits `js`/`jsx`. The repo contains `svelte.config.js` (a real, tracked JS file), and no pattern in this config matches `*.js`, so that file is silently skipped by both prettier and eslint at commit time while every sibling config file (`.ts`, `.mjs`) is formatted. Same applies to any future `*.jsx`. Note this is a gap in the glob key itself (not the command values), so a typo/omission here silently drops coverage with no error. comments.content: `copyLoader()` is a single manual call site in each branch (build and watch), so nothing guarantees the copy happens on *every* rebuild path: in watch mode it runs exactly once right before `ctx.watch()`, so editing `src/loader.cjs` afterwards never refreshes `dist/loader.cjs` and the running extension keeps loading a stale loader while the bundle is rebuilt — a silent drift that is easy to miss in dev. Any new build path (e.g. a plugin, or a `--watch`+CI hybrid) can also silently forget the copy, and the explanatory comment above the function must then drift out of sync with the call sites. The robust fix is an esbuild plugin (e.g. `onStart`) so the copy is guaranteed to run on every rebuild instead of being duplicated across manual call sites.

**False green: a stale report decides this run's exit code.** The suite *appends* its summary to whatever is already in the file (`src/test/suite/index.ts`: `existing + lines.join("\n")`), and this script never removes the previous run's report. The unanchored `/FAIL:\s*(\d+)/` takes the **first** match in the file, which is the *oldest* run's line.

Concretely: run 1 leaves `PASS: 120  FAIL: 0`; run 2 fails 3 tests, so the file becomes `PASS: 120  FAIL: 0\nPASS: 117  FAIL: 3\n...`. This block matches `FAIL: 0`, evaluates `Number("0") > 0` as false, and calls `process.exit(0)` — **3 failing tests reported as success.** The inverse (stale `FAIL: 3` + a green run) yields a bogus red, and a crashed/crashed-early run leaves the old verdict in place so the watchdog reads it as authoritative. The unanchored regex also mis-matches detail lines like `FAIL: 3 retries: ...` (the suite writes `FAIL: ${test.fullTitle()}` per failure).

`runTest.ts` already solves this for the same report: it `rmSync`s the report before the run (line 175) and `isGreenReport()` requires both an mtime newer than the run start and the anchored `/^PASS: \d+\s+FAIL: (\d+)$/m`. Do the same here: clear the report before the run (this also gives an mtime-freshness check something meaningful to compare against) and use the same authority rule. Requires `statSync` added to the `node:fs` import and a `runStartedAt` timestamp captured before `mod.run()`.

The rejection is logged and then discarded: no `process.exitCode` is set and no failure flag is recorded. The comment claims "a crashed run without one must not exit 0", but that only holds because of the 20s timeout — and once the report is cleared (see the sibling comment), a crash leaves no report and the timeout is the only guard. More importantly, this *overrides* the suite's own crash signal: `src/test/suite/index.ts` installs `uncaughtException`/`unhandledRejection` handlers that append `UNCAUGHT:`/`UNHANDLED:` lines and set `process.exitCode = 1`. The `process.exit(0)` in the watchdog block below discards that `exitCode`, so a run that logged an uncaught exception but had 0 mocha failures still exits 0. Record the crash and make the final verdict honour it.

These paths are resolved against `process.cwd()`, not the repository. That only works because `package.json` happens to invoke the script from the root. If the script is ever run from another directory (a sub-package, an IDE task, a CI step with a different cwd) the suite — which writes its report to `path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, "test-results.log")`, i.e. next to the compiled `index.js` — writes to a *different* absolute path than the one polled at line 53, so the watchdog waits out its full timeout and reports failure despite a green suite. Anchor the paths to the script location via `import.meta.dirname` / `fileURLToPath` so cwd no longer matters.

comments.content: The `.svelte` short-circuit applies to *any* specifier ending in `.svelte`, not just file paths. A bare package subpath such as `some-lib/Comp.svelte` (or `@scope/pkg/Comp.svelte`) is turned into `<importerDir>/some-lib/Comp.svelte`, producing a bogus URL that later fails with a raw `ENOENT` in the load hook instead of being delegated to the default resolver. The same happens for specifiers carrying a query/hash suffix (e.g. `./Comp.svelte?raw`), because the suffix is treated as part of the filename. Also, the existence of the file is never verified here, so a typo'd path only surfaces as an opaque `readFileSync` error. Restrict the branch to path-like specifiers (`.`/`/`/`file:`) and let everything else fall through to `nextResolve`.

Two independent, mismatched hardcoded extension lists live in this file: `[".ts", ".js", ".json"]` here (the "already resolvable" set) and `[".ts", ".js", ".svelte"]` in `probeExtensions`. Adding an extension requires editing both places, and the mismatch is already observable: the probe never tries `.mjs`/`.cjs`, while a specifier such as `./utils.mjs` is still treated as extensionless and burns three failing `nextResolve` calls. Extract the lists into named constants so the probe and the predicate stay in sync.

The bare `catch` discards every resolution error, so when a workspace import is genuinely missing or misnamed, the developer only sees the default resolver's `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` with no indication that `.ts`/`.js`/`.svelte` siblings were already probed. Keep the failure reasons (at least the last error per candidate) so a fully-failed probe can throw a message listing what was tried, which makes typo'd imports diagnosable.

Both the preprocess map and `compile(...).js.map` are computed and then discarded, so no source mapping is emitted at all. A Svelte compile error or a runtime failure inside a component will report stack frames pointing at generated component code rather than the original `.svelte` source, which is exactly the DX this loader exists to provide. Since Node's loader does not consume a returned map, the practical fix is to append the compiled map to the emitted source as an inline `sourceMappingURL` comment (ideally composed with the preprocess map).

No error handling around `readFileSync`/`preprocess`/`compile`: a missing file or a preprocessing failure escapes the loader as a bare stack trace. Combined with the unchecked `.svelte` short-circuit in `resolve`, a mis-resolved path shows up as an unexplained `ENOENT` with no indication of which file the test tried to load. Wrap the pipeline and rethrow with the filename and the original error as `cause`. The `.svelte.js` branch has the same gap.

`runes: true` is hardcoded here, duplicating `compilerOptions.runes` from `svelte.config.js`. If the app config changes (runes toggled, extra compiler options such as `dev` or custom `warningFilter`), the test loader silently keeps the old behaviour and diverges from what Vite compiles. Import the repository config (or read the shared `svelte.config.js`) instead of restating its values.

The file header states the regression is "count showed but the view never moved to the phrase", but nothing in the suite asserts that the view moved. In jsdom `getBoundingClientRect()` returns all-zero rects, so `scrollToMatch()` always takes the `offsetTop` fallback, which is also `0` in jsdom — the container's `scrollTop` can never be observed to change, so the original bug could return and this suite would still pass (it only checks the counter text and CSS classes, which are set independently of the scroll write).

Make the scroll observable by stubbing a non-zero box on the messages container *before* typing, then assert `scrollTop` moves to the target after next/prev.

The suite's central invariant is "count must correspond to a visible target", but the second test never cross-checks the count against the number of rendered highlights, nor that the *current* mark (`mark.search-highlight-current`, the class `scrollToMatch` toggles) actually follows navigation. A regression that moves the counter/wrapper class but leaves the highlighted phrase behind would pass. Also note `marks.length >= 1` in the first test is redundant with the following `.some()` assertion.

`const [prev, next] = querySelectorAll(".search-nav")` couples the test to DOM order. The component already exposes `aria-label="Previous match"` / `"Next match"`, so selecting by label removes the ambiguity: with positional destructuring, a markup reorder swaps prev/next and the assertions fail with a misleading "2/2 vs 0/2" message rather than naming the button. Note also that `assert.ok(prev, ...)` is only reached after the next-button assertions, so a missing prev button fails late.

comments.content: `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(proto, "value")` throws a TypeError if `proto` is `undefined` (it is not null-guarded), and the `else input.value = text` fallback silently degrades the test: without the native setter, Svelte's `bind:value` may never observe the change and the failure surfaces later as a confusing `1/1` vs `0 matches` mismatch instead of pointing at the harness. Assert the setter exists so a broken environment fails at the point of the mistake.

`flush()` burns a fixed number of `setTimeout(0)` rounds, which is timing-sensitive: any debounce, throttled search, or extra `tick()`/`$effect` chain added to `scrollToMatch()` (which is already `async` and awaits `tick()`) makes the suite fail intermittently or — worse — pass only because the window happens to be wide enough. Poll for the expected state instead so the wait is both deterministic and self-documenting.

Every webview spec re-implements its own jsdom bootstrap that permanently re-points `globalThis.window`/`document` (plus constructors, `navigator`, rAF) at import time with no restore step, and the blocks are near-verbatim copies with drifting variations. Because `scripts/run-webview-tests.mjs` imports all four specs into **one** Mocha process before `mocha.run()`, the last spec imported overwrites the globals that earlier specs' components and `@testing-library/svelte` were loaded against, making the suite order-dependent and dependent on import order; `chat-search.test.mjs` even reads back the `globalThis.window` installed by an earlier spec, and its own guarded branch adopts a pre-existing window without ever assigning `globalThis.document` (a host defining only `window` would leave `document` undefined and crash the component on import).

Extract the block into a single idempotent shared harness (e.g. `scripts/webview-test-harness.mjs` / `webview/test-dom-setup.mjs`) that exports the dom instance and installs/restores the globals, imported once by the runner *before* any spec import, and have each spec import it. Reuse one definition so fixes (e.g. adding `requestAnimationFrame`, `CSS`, `MutationObserver`) are not repeated across four files.

The rAF shim is a half-implementation: it is driven by Node's `setTimeout`/`setTimeout`-like handle, so the value passed to the callback is a Node `Timeout` object (or a jsdom timer id on the other spec) rather than a numeric handle, and no matching `cancelAnimationFrame` is installed. A component that does the standard `const h = requestAnimationFrame(...); cancelAnimationFrame(h)` pair will throw a TypeError (or silently fail to cancel, and the callback runs with a non-numeric timestamp, which makes `flush()` timing-dependent). Provide both halves of the pair and drive it from the window's own timer domain so handles and `clearTimeout` agree.

After a model switch the session keeps running the *unsupported* thinking level on the backend while the header/settings UI asserts the fallback is active, so the real session state is misreported and the drift persists until the user manually re-picks a level. Either propagate the clamp to the parent (`onThinkingLevelChange(levels[0])`), or surface it as an explicit warning state instead of masking it. This click-outside logic is duplicated verbatim for the favorites dropdown and only handles `click`. There is no `Escape` handler, so once opened a dropdown can only be dismissed with a mouse outside click — keyboard-only users can get stuck with an open popup. `.filter(Boolean)` followed by `as Model[]` launders the `(Model | undefined)[]` result, hiding the unresolved entries from the type checker. Svelte's keyed each will: create a new item for key N (new message), destroy the item for key 0, and for keys 1..N-1, reuse the DOM nodes but update the `message` prop (the component's `message` prop changes from messages[k] to messages[k-1]). `height`/`width` are defaulted to `"auto"`/`"100%"` here, which makes every `||` fallback in the `circle` and `bar` branches unreachable (`"auto"` and `"100%"` are both truthy). With default props:

comments.content: The toggle is wrapped in a `<label class="toggle">` that contains only the hidden input and the slider span, so the control has no accessible name — screen readers announce an unlabelled switch; the descriptive text lives in a sibling `.tool-info`/label-text div that is not associated with the input. `toSkillInfo` blindly trusts every field of a record that arrives from an unvalidated payload. `s.name` throws if `s` is `null`/`undefined`, and if `name` ends up non-string (e.g. a number or object from a malformed message) the *derived* `filteredSkills` then calls `s.name.toLowerCase()` and blows up during render, taking down the whole panel. `toSkillInfo` is also applied to `data.skills` from the `sessionResources` prop, so the same risk exists on the prop path.

Coerce with the `asString` helper so every field is guaranteed to be a string, and fall back to a stable key when `name` is absent.

Identity is tracked by `skill.name`, but the host deliberately supplies a separate unique `key` (`toWebviewSkill` → `key: this.skillToggleKey(s)`) precisely because names are not unique across packages/sources, and the merged `getAllSkills()` list keeps both colliding rows. With duplicate keys the keyed `{#each}` throws `Cannot have duplicate keys in a keyed each block` in dev and reuses the wrong DOM node in production (stale descriptions/badges after refresh). Expansion state has the same collision: expanding one same-named skill expands all of them, and the matching `{#if expandedSkill === skill.name}` can render no details at all. Use `skill.key` everywhere — list key, `expandSkill()` and the template comparison — which also agrees with `toggleSkill`, which already sends `skill.key` to the host.

comments.existing_code: {#each filteredSkills as skill (skill.name)}

comments.content:
`skills` has three competing writers: this effect, the `skills-list` handler, and the `session-resources` handler. Because the effect re-runs on every change of the `sessionResources` prop *identity* and unconditionally re-maps the array, a parent re-render that recreates the object will clobber a fresher list pushed by the host, and each remap allocates a new array that invalidates the keyed `{#each}` — causing full-list DOM churn on every parent update.

Guard on the actual payload instead of the object identity so the effect is a no-op when the skills haven't really changed.

`outputText` is only ever appended to and never truncated, and it is re-assigned on every `output` message, so a long-running install/uninstall can grow it without bound — a large string re-rendered into the `<pre>` on each chunk is a real jank source in the webview. It is only reset when the user hits "Close".

Separately, the overlay can latch on permanently: `removeSkillPackage` sets `showLoadingOverlay = true` and the dialog is only dismissed when a `loading:false` message arrives or the user clicks Close. If the host errors out without emitting that message, the modal (`position: fixed; inset: 0`) blocks the entire panel. Cap the buffer and add a defensive reset.

SkillsPanel's loading timers are created but never stored or cleared: the 2s deadline in `refreshSkills()` and the 100ms `setTimeout(refreshSkills)` in the `loading` message handler (which itself starts another uncleaned timer), so every refresh/`removeSkillPackage` leaks timers that can fire after unmount and mutate `isLoading`/`showLoadingOverlay` on a destroyed component. Worse, `isLoading` is force-cleared at 2s whether or not the host ever replied, so a session with many skills leaves the "Loading skills…" branch and renders the actively misleading "No skills loaded" empty state. Keep the timer ids, clear the previous one before re-arming, clear both on destroy, and clear `isLoading` when data actually arrives rather than on a fixed deadline.

Raw, unvalidated user text is forwarded to the host, and the host does no validation either: `message-handler.ts:465` passes `payload.paths` straight through to `setExtraSkillPaths`, which writes them verbatim into the global `pi-agent.extraSkills` setting and immediately calls `reloadSessionResources()`. A `~`-prefixed or relative path is also stored unresolved, so `~/a` and `/home/me/a` become two near-duplicate entries that both get scanned on every reload.

Normalize/expand the path and require an absolute form before sending, and reject rather than silently persist unusable entries.

`getVsCodeApi` is a byte-identical copy of the one in `PiPackagesPanel.svelte` and `SettingsPanel.svelte` (the project already consolidated the sibling `postToHost` helper into `messages.ts` for exactly this reason). Beyond duplication, this is fragile: `acquireVsCodeApi()` may only be called **once** per webview lifetime and throws on a second call, so the only thing keeping it safe is that `App.svelte` happens to cache onto `window.vscode` first — an ordering dependency with no `try/catch`. Note `postToHost` already reads the cached `window.vscode`, and the return value here is never used by the caller, so this can be dropped and the shared helper reused.

`isLoading` is only ever cleared inside the `system-prompt` message handler, but the host does not always answer. `PiAgentProvider.sendSystemPrompt()` (src/pi-agent-provider.ts:3191) starts with `if (!this.session) return;` — it posts nothing when there is no active session, and `postToHost` silently no-ops when `window.vscode` is unavailable. The only other push is on `agent_start` (src/pi-agent-provider.ts:2792). So on the most common entry path — opening this tab before a session/run exists — the panel spins on "Loading system prompt…" indefinitely, and the actionable empty state written specifically for that case ("Start a session (e.g. send a message)…") is unreachable. `sessionResources` is already passed in and is `null` when no session exists, so the panel can decide this locally instead of guessing. Add a bounded wait as a backstop too.

Replies are accepted unconditionally, with no request or session identity check. This effect fires a fresh `getSystemPrompt` on every `sessionResources` change, but the panel neither clears the previous prompt nor resets `isLoading`, so during a session switch/restart the old session's prompt stays on screen and the Copy button stays enabled — a user can copy the previous session's prompt believing it is the current one. Worse, a late reply for the previous request can land after the new request was issued and overwrite the current prompt permanently. `postToHost`/`system-prompt` carries no id today, but a panel-local counter still drops out-of-order replies (postMessage preserves host-side ordering); the complete fix is for the host to include a session id in the `system-prompt` payload.

The feedback timer is never tracked or cleared. Two consequences: (1) repeated clicks stack timers, so an early timer resets `copyState` to "idle" while a later copy's feedback is still on screen (click at t=0, click at t=1500 → "Copied!" disappears after 0.5s instead of 2s); (2) the timer survives component teardown, writing state to a destroyed component. Store the handle, clear it before re-arming, and clear it on destroy.

`any` erases all type checking for the only prop this component consumes, and the prop is not actually read — it is used purely as a reactive dependency trigger via `void sessionResources`. Most sibling panels declare a named `Props` type; declare the real shape (or a minimal `{ sessionId?: string }`-style type) so a malformed payload is caught at compile time and the intent is documented.
comments.suggestion_code:
type Props = { sessionResources?: { sessionId?: string } | null };
  let { sessionResources = null }: Props = $props();
comments.existing_code: let { sessionResources = null }: { sessionResources?: any } = $props();

comments.content: The existing spec (src/test/webview/system-prompt-panel.test.mjs) only ever pushes a well-formed `system-prompt` message, so the two most fragile paths in this handler are uncovered: (a) no message ever arrives (the host returns early when no session exists) — nothing asserts that the panel leaves the loading state; (b) a second `getSystemPrompt` request followed by two out-of-order replies — nothing asserts which prompt wins. Neither `copyState = "fail"` nor the 2s feedback reset is covered either. Since the component is already mountable in jsdom, adding these cases is cheap and would have caught both bugs above.

Cap eviction ignores `persistent`. `toasts[0]` may be a toast the caller explicitly marked `persistent: true` (i.e. "must not auto-dismiss"), yet it is silently removed here while a newer auto-dismissing toast survives — and the caller's `dismissToast`-less "sticky" toast vanishes with no feedback. Evict the oldest *non-persistent* toast first. Also, `if` only removes one entry; using `while` keeps the invariant correct even if the list is ever over the cap by more than one.

The comment contradicts the code. It claims `NaN`/`Infinity`/no-duration "mean no auto dismiss", but the implementation maps all of those to `30000`, i.e. an *active* 30s auto-dismiss. The same surprise applies to `duration: 0` or a negative value, which callers may pass intending "sticky" but get a 30s dismissal. Either fix the comment to describe the real behaviour, or honour an explicit non-positive/`Infinity` duration as "no auto dismiss" so `persistent` is not the only opt-out.

The `!(window as any).__toast` guard makes ownership acquisition non-deterministic and can permanently break toasts:
- If a previous instance registered the global and is destroyed *after* this instance's script runs (exactly what Svelte HMR remount does), this instance skips registration, and then the old instance's cleanup still matches (`__toast.showToast === oldShowToast`) and deletes the global. `window.__toast` is then permanently `undefined` and every `showToast` call in `App.svelte` / `ProviderSettings.svelte` silently no-ops.
- Symmetrically, if an old instance is torn down without its cleanup running, the new instance inherits a reference bound to discarded `$state` and renders nothing.

Always take ownership in the new instance; the cleanup is already written to only delete the global when it still points at this instance, so it stays safe.

Accessibility problems in the live region:
1. `role="alert"` implies an assertive, atomic announcement of the element's *accessible name*. Because `aria-labelledby` points only at the title, `toast.message` is never announced to screen readers.
2. `role="alert"` (assertive) nested inside the `aria-live="polite"` container defeats the intended politeness and causes the toast plus the dismiss button label to be announced twice/interruptingly.
3. The container is only rendered `{#if toasts.length > 0}`, so the live region does not exist in the DOM before the first toast is inserted — several screen readers never announce the initial insertion.

Simplest fix: keep a single polite live region that always exists and let the toast content be read (no `role="alert"`, no `aria-labelledby` overriding it).
comments.suggestion_code: <div class="toast toast-{toast.type}">
comments.existing_code: <div class="toast toast-{toast.type}" role="alert" aria-labelledby="{toast.id}-title">

comments.content: `src/webview/app.d.ts` already declares `Window.__toast` with this exact shape, so these `(window as any)` casts throw away type checking (a typo like `showToasts` or a wrong option key would still compile). Use the declared global directly, consistent with the typed `Window` surface.

comments.content:
`notifyToolChange()` unconditionally force-switches the preset to `"custom"`, but it is also called by `applyPreset(preset)` with `notify = true` — which is exactly the path used by every preset card. Clicking "Default", "Review Only" or "None" therefore sets `toolPreset = preset`, then immediately overwrites it with `"custom"` and persists `toolPreset: "custom"`. The host echoes the change back (`message-handler.ts:763` sends `settings-response`), so `propPreset` becomes `"custom"` too and the panel ends up permanently stuck on the Custom card: the other three presets are unreachable from the UI.

Force the switch to `"custom"` only for genuinely manual per-tool edits, and let an explicit preset selection keep its own name.

comments.content:
This effect reads `toolPreset`, so `toolPreset` becomes a tracked dependency and the effect re-runs on every *local* change too, not just on parent-driven ones (contradicting the comment above). When the user applies a preset, `notifyToolChange()` sets `toolPreset = "custom"` while `propPreset` is still the old value until the host's `settings-response` arrives; the effect fires in between and runs `applyPreset(propPreset, false)`, wiping the just-applied state. For example, after clicking "Review Only" the panel briefly flips to the default preset with all 7 tools enabled, and it settles with all tools shown as enabled while the session actually runs read-only.

Only react to an actual change of `propPreset` (compare against the previously seen value) instead of treating local state as a trigger.

The non-`custom` branches rebuild `tools` from `defaultTools` only, so every user-added custom tool is discarded when a preset is applied. Because `applyPreset` then calls `notifyToolChange()`, the reduced built-in list is also written back to `pi-agent.customTools`, permanently deleting the user's custom tool names from global settings (the `source` field and any custom entries are lost with no warning).

Preserve the custom entries across preset switches, e.g. `const custom = tools.filter((t) => t.category !== "builtin")` and append them to the preset-derived built-ins.

`index` here is the index inside the *filtered* `builtinTools` array, but `toggleTool(index)` maps it onto the unfiltered `tools` array. It happens to line up today only because built-ins are always stored first and custom tools are appended; any reordering, a restored custom tool, or a future `sort`/insert turns this into a silent wrong-tool toggle. The custom-tools block below already does the correct lookup by name — use the same approach here.

comments.content:
Custom tool names are accepted with only trim + lowercase: no charset, length, or format validation. The name is persisted verbatim into the user's global `pi-agent.customTools` setting and passed to the runtime as a tool identifier, so arbitrary strings (whitespace, separators, very long values, control characters) end up in settings and can break downstream tool resolution/logging. Rendering is safe (Svelte escapes the interpolation), but the input contract should still be constrained — and the current code rejects duplicates/invalid input *silently*, giving the user no feedback.

Validate against an identifier pattern, cap the length, and surface an error instead of a no-op.

const name = customToolsInput.trim().toLowerCase();
    if (!name || tools.some((t) => t.name === name)) return;

comments.content: The panel requests `getSettings` but only ever receives `toolPreset` (App.svelte stores just that field), so the persisted `customTools` list is never restored here. A session started with `toolPreset: "custom"` therefore displays only the built-ins, while the header still shows the "Synced" badge; the next toggle then overwrites `pi-agent.customTools` with just the built-in names, wiping the stored custom tools. Accept the persisted tool list (e.g. a `customTools` prop or a `settings-response` handler) and rebuild `tools` from it, and only show "Synced" when the full tool set is known to match.

The banner is rendered whenever `lightMode` is true, but the restriction only applies when `toolPreset === "default"` (see `lightRestrictsTools`, matching `pi-agent-provider.ts:932-938`). Under "Review Only" / "None" / "Custom" the runtime honors the explicit preset instead, so the message ("Only read, bash, edit and write are active") is false. Also note `LIGHT_MODE_TOOLS` duplicates the list hard-coded in the provider, so the two can drift.

Render the restricted copy only when `lightRestrictsTools`, otherwise describe the active preset.

comments.content: `sendToolUpdate` is fire-and-forget: `vscode.postMessage` returns a promise that is neither awaited nor error-handled, and the host's error response (sent by `withErrorReporting` in `message-handler.ts:761`) is ignored. If persisting `pi-agent.toolPreset` / `pi-agent.customTools` fails, the panel still shows the new state with no error, so the UI silently diverges from the session. Consider awaiting the post and reverting/refreshing on failure (the host already echoes `settings-response`, which can be used as the confirmation signal).

The bare `catch {}` discards the error with no diagnostics, so a broken/unreadable git repo is indistinguishable from "not a git repository" and is impossible to debug from logs. Consider surfacing it (inject an optional `onError`/logger, as the provider already has `logError`).

`resolveGitBranch` performs blocking, synchronous filesystem I/O on the shared extension-host thread: it performs `existsSync` + `statSync` on every ancestor directory, then `existsSync` + `readFileSync` on `HEAD` (two filesystem round-trips per check where one would do), with no depth limit and no caching of the last resolved repo root.

It is called from `src/footer-manager.ts:56` on a 5-second polling interval, so on a deep tree or a network/remote mount (SSH, WSL, SMB) this blocks the extension host every tick, forever, with no back-off. Drop the redundant `existsSync` calls and let the surrounding `try/catch` handle the miss; cache the resolved git dir per `cwd` and short-circuit subsequent calls, and/or watch `.git/HEAD` with `fs.watch` and/or raise the poll interval.

The original PATH is never stashed on the instance, so callers must capture and thread `process.env.PATH` by hand before calling `prependToPath()`; any future caller that forgets has no way to undo the mutation. This `.catch` can never fire: `resolveCliModelIds()` already ends with its own `.catch` that swallows every failure (including the `code !== 0` throw) and resolves with `new Set<string>()`. Two consequences:

1. The recovery path documented in the comment is dead code — the failure never reaches here, so `cliModelIdsPromise` is never reset.
2. The empty set returned on failure flows into the `.then` above and **is** memoized into `cliModelIdsCache`, which is precisely the "favorites sync permanently dead until an explicit invalidate" bug the comment says it prevents. `syncFavoritesToSettings()` and `syncFromCliModels()` both bail out on `size === 0`, so a single transient CLI failure (missing PATH entry, 15s timeout) disables favorites sync for the whole session.

Fix: don't memoize an empty result, and let failures reach the outer catch (rethrow from `resolveCliModelIds` or have it resolve `null` on failure).

Race with an in-flight resolution: both fields are nulled, but the already-pending `resolveCliModelIds().then(ids => { this.cliModelIdsCache = ids; })` in `getCliModelIds` still fires afterwards and repopulates the cache with the **pre-invalidation** model list. Since `cliModelIdsPromise` is now `null`, nothing re-triggers a fetch, so the stale list is used for the rest of the session — exactly what the cache is meant to survive (auth change → new models available). This is reachable from `pi-agent-provider.refreshModels()`, which calls `invalidateCliModelIdsCache()` right before a `refresh`.

Guard the cache write with a generation counter so results from a superseded resolution are discarded.

`setEnabledModels()` replaces the whole `enabledModels` array, so filtering the extension favorites against `cliModels` and writing the result is a destructive overwrite of user config. Any favorite the CLI doesn't report (CLI version mismatch, a provider just added to models.json, partially parsed `--list-models` output, ANSI-polluted ids) is silently deleted from settings.json with no log and no way to recover. This also directly fights `syncFromCliModels()` above, whose whole purpose is to import models the user enabled in PI CLI (Ctrl+P): toggling one favorite in the webview can wipe the CLI-side selection out from under the user.

Safer: union with the models already enabled in the CLI, and/or log the dropped patterns so the loss is visible.

No error handling: if `modelRegistry.refresh()` or `getAvailable()` rejects (corrupt models.json, disk/permission error), the rejection escapes to callers — `pi-agent-provider.refreshModels()` and the startup init path — and `notifyWebview` is never called, so the webview keeps showing a stale/empty model list with no feedback. `logError` is already available on deps for exactly this. Two problems with the CLI output parsing:

1. Concatenating `stderr` into the parsed text contradicts the comment two lines above ("shell error text on stderr is never parsed as a model table"). The regex `^(\S+)\s+(\S+)\s+\S` matches *any* line with three tokens, so an `npm WARN ...`, `Error: cannot find module ...`, or version-mismatch warning is turned into a bogus `provider/model` id. The only guard is `match[0].startsWith("Warning")`, which filters a single literal prefix.
2. ANSI escape codes are not stripped. `stripAnsi()` is already exported from `./utils/shell.js` and this same file imports from it — colored CLI output (very likely for a table) makes `match[1]`/provider ids contain escape sequences, corrupting every parsed id and breaking the `cliModels.has(pattern)` checks in both sync methods.

`findPiBinary()` can return values that never pass through `isSafeBinaryPath`, even though callers hand the result to `execFileAsync(..., { shell: true })`.

(1) The win32 probe does it explicitly: `where` is a real executable, not a shell builtin, so `shell: true` is not needed — and it hands `binary` to cmd.exe, which re-parses it. This branch is reached with whatever `findPiBinary()` returned (including the literal `"pi"` fallthrough and any relative candidate from an unset env var), and unlike the POSIX branch there is no `isSafeBinaryPath` guard, so a name carrying `&`, `%`, `^`, `!` or a quote reaches the shell.
(2) The PATH-scan branch only validates the *setting-derived* path via `resolvePiBinaryFromSetting()`; `dir` comes from `process.env.PATH` and `binary` may be the `"pi"`/well-known-candidate fallthrough, so `path.join(dir, binary)` is never passed through `isSafeBinaryPath`.

Apply the same guard to every value these paths can emit, and drop `shell: true` from the `where` probe.

When neither `HOME` nor `USERPROFILE` is set, `home` is `""` and every home-based candidate collapses to a CWD-relative path (`path.join("", ".local/bin/pi")` → `.local/bin/pi`). `accessSync` then probes those relative paths against the extension host's working directory, so a repository that ships `.local/bin/pi` (or `.bun/bin/pi`, `.npm-global/bin/pi`, …) can be picked up and later spawned. Short-circuit when the home directory is unknown, and skip candidates whose base env var is unset (same issue applies to the Windows `LOCALAPPDATA`/`APPDATA`/`ProgramFiles` entries).

The identical pattern is repeated at the end of `performCheckWithDeduplication` (~line 505). Await the dialog and wrap the dispatch in try/catch as the other call sites do.

`DefaultPackageManager.checkForAvailableUpdates()` spawns git/npm subprocesses and has no timeout, unlike the `fetch` path which uses `AbortSignal.timeout`. Combined with the `catch { return [] }` below, a hung or failing package check is silently reported as "no updates" and cannot be distinguished from "up to date" — and `performCheckWithDeduplication` then persists `STORAGE_KEY_LAST_CHECK`, so the failure costs a full throttle window. Also `u.type as "npm" | "git"` is an unchecked assertion that will happily pass any other upstream value. Add a timeout, log the error, and validate `type` before casting.

Re-entrancy hazard: there is no in-flight guard around `performCheckWithDeduplication`. The throttle is read from `globalState` at the start and only written after all the awaits, so two overlapping invocations (initial 15s timer plus the interval, or a manual trigger) both observe a stale `lastCheck` and both proceed to fetch, persist state, and show duplicate notifications. `dispose()` also does not cancel an in-flight check. Add a module-level in-flight flag/latch around the check.

Behaviour drift between the two check paths: `runUpdateCheck` deliberately uses `pi update --extensions` when only package updates exist, but this path always runs the full `pi update` (which can also upgrade/alter the CLI) even for package-only updates. Use the same conditional dispatch here.

Substantial duplication: the details building, the `switch (action)` dispatch and the entire "View Details" second-dialog flow are duplicated between `runUpdateCheck` and `performCheckWithDeduplication` (~80 lines), and the copies have already drifted (one shows `pkg.packageName`, the other doesn't; the other has the extensions-only auto-update path). Extract a single helper (e.g. `promptForUpdates(piUpdate, packageUpdates)` + `dispatchUpdateAction(action)`) and call it from both.

Offline gating is inconsistent. The background path checks the `pi-agent.offline` setting, but this manual path only inherits the `PI_OFFLINE` / `PI_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK` env-var checks buried inside `fetchLatestPiRelease` and `checkForPackageUpdates` — so the manual "Check for Updates" command still hits the network while the user has offline mode enabled. Read the same setting here and pass it down (or reuse a shared guard).

Deduplication state is persisted *before* the user has seen or acted on the notification. If the notification is dismissed, or if auto-update is enabled and the terminal update fails, the update is permanently recorded as "known" and is never re-reported (until `clearKnownUpdates` is called manually). Persist only after a confirmed action, or store an attempt/timestamp so the checker can re-nag.

comments.content:
Destructive/losing fallback in the v11→v12 swap. Two data-loss paths here:
1. `fs.rmSync(backupDir, { recursive: true, force: true })` unconditionally deletes any pre-existing `<dir>.bak-v11` — a backup created by an earlier repair (or a user directory that happens to share the name) is destroyed without warning.
2. If `renameSync` fails (e.g. cross-device link, locked file on Windows), the code falls back to `fs.rmSync(brokenDir, { recursive: true, force: true })`, permanently deleting the user's installed module *before* the symlink is attempted. If `symlinkSync` then also fails, the restore path only looks for `backupDir`, which no longer exists, so the module is gone for good.

Since `tryUpgradeToV12` is only reached after a failed rebuild, a mere tooling failure (missing `node-gyp`/`prebuild-install`) can wipe a working install. Keep the original directory at all costs and abort the upgrade if it can't be set aside.

`checkBetterSqlite3` returns `ok: false` when **zero** copies are found (`firstMismatch === null && copies.length > 0`). For users who have no `~/.pi/agent/npm` install at all, `ensureBetterSqlite3Compatible` therefore falls through to `rebuildBetterSqlite3()`, which returns `success: false, output: "No better-sqlite3 copies found"`. The caller (`pi-agent-provider.checkNativeAddons` / `rebuildNativeAddons`) then logs/shows a user-facing "Native addon ABI mismatch … Auto-rebuild failed" error on every startup. "Nothing installed" must not be reported as an ABI mismatch.

`spawnSync` runs on the extension-host thread, so the whole host is frozen for the duration: up to 30 s for `prebuild-install` plus 300 s for `node-gyp` **per copy** (up to two copies) on every `checkNativeAddons()` invocation at startup and on the manual rebuild path. The `withProgress` notification in the caller cannot even paint while this is blocking. Use an async `execFile`/`spawn` + `await` so the event loop stays alive.

`prebuild-install` can exit 0 while downloading nothing (no prebuilt binary for that Electron/arch combination prints a message and, depending on the config, still succeeds). Because `tryPrebuildInstall` returns `""` (non-null) in that case, this branch short-circuits and returns `success: true`, so strategy 2 (`node-gyp`) is never attempted and the v11→v12 fallback in `rebuildBetterSqlite3` is never reached either. Validate the binary before declaring success, otherwise fall through.

When the rebuild "succeeds" but the ABI verification still fails, only `allOk` and the message are updated — the entry pushed into the public `results` array keeps `success: true` and the raw build output. Callers that inspect `results` (see `ensureBetterSqlite3Compatible`'s `anyRebuilt`) therefore see a broken copy reported as successfully rebuilt. Mark the entry as failed for consistency.

comments.content: `rebuilt` is derived by substring-matching the human-readable build log for `"already compatible"`. A compiler log line that happens to contain that phrase (or a future wording change) flips the flag. The results array should carry an explicit discriminator, e.g. `action: "already-ok" | "rebuilt" | "upgraded" | "failed"`, instead of parsing free text.

Architecture is hardcoded to `x64` (here and in the `prebuild-install --arch x64` argument). On arm64 hosts (Apple Silicon, arm64 Electron) this downloads/compiles a binary for the wrong architecture, so the ABI verification afterwards fails, the copy is reported as broken, and the next startup repeats the whole multi-minute rebuild. Derive the arch from the runtime.

Both spawned tools are resolved as `<targetDir>/node_modules/.bin/{prebuild-install,node-gyp}` and executed with `process.execPath` (node). Problems: (a) on Windows npm only creates `.cmd`/`.ps1` shims, so `node node_modules\.bin\node-gyp` cannot resolve the file at all; (b) neither `prebuild-install` nor `node-gyp` is a runtime dependency of better-sqlite3 (they are devDependencies), so the path frequently does not exist in an installed copy. Both failures are swallowed and fall through to the destructive `tryUpgradeToV12` swap, turning a "tooling missing" condition into a module replacement. Resolve the tool via `require.resolve`/`npx` and, at minimum, distinguish "tool not found" from "build failed" so the destructive path is not taken.

comments.content: `abi === null` conflates three very different states: the `.node` file is missing, it is unreadable, or the `node_register_module_v*` symbol lies beyond the 256 KB probe window. All three are marked `compatible: false`, so a perfectly good module can trigger a multi-minute rebuild and — if that fails — the destructive v11→v12 directory swap. Use a tri-state (`compatible` / `mismatch` / `unknown`) and only run the upgrade path on a real mismatch.

comments.content: The ABI→Node mapping is a hardcoded table that will silently go stale, and the Electron entries are guesses: reporting ABI 140 as "22.x (Electron build)" describes an Electron-specific ABI in terms of a Node major, which is misleading — the module was built for Electron 39, not Node 22. Prefer deriving the label from the live runtime (`process.versions.node` / `process.versions.electron`) for the runtime side and only using the table for legacy Node ABIs, with a clear "Electron ABI (unmapped to Node)" fallback.

`(window as any).vscode` defeats the typing that the project already provides: `src/webview/app.d.ts` declares a global `Window.vscode?: VsCodeApi` (with an explicit comment "no `any` in component code"). The `as any` cast here disables all type checking on the bridge call and contradicts the project rule against `any`. Dropping the cast gives a compile-time-checked `vscode?.postMessage(...)` call.

The `typeof === "function"` guard can be kept (it still defends against a forged `window.vscode` value), but it does not need the `any` cast to compile.
comments.thinking:
Key findings:

1. `app.d.ts` already declares `Window.vscode?: VsCodeApi` globally, so `(window as any).vscode` in `postToHost` is unnecessary `any` usage — the checklist explicitly prohibits `any`. This is a real, actionable finding: drop the `as any` cast. Also note the project doc says "no `any` in component code" — the comment in app.d.ts line 4 explicitly states "Structural view of the VS Code webview API bridge (no `any` in component code)". So this file violates that. Good finding.

Also `typeof vscode?.postMessage === "function"` — the guard is redundant given the type, but defensive. Actually with the typed declaration, `vscode?.postMessage` check suffices. But keeping `typeof ... === "function"` is fine for defense against a forged `window.vscode` object. Keep it but with typed access.

2. `clampNumber` fallback is not clamped to [min, max] — documented behavior says "Clamp a number into [min, max], returning fallback for non-finite input or invalid bounds". If fallback is out of range (e.g. fallback=200, min=0, max=100), the function returns 200, violating the clamp contract. This is a genuine edge-case bug. Medium/low. The callers here pass 0 which is in range, so impact is low. I'll report as low/medium bug.

3. `parseHostMessage` doesn't validate origin/source — the header comment says only the extension host is the legitimate sender, but there's no check on `event.origin` / `event.source`. Since this is a shared guard, hardening it here (allow-list `vscode-webview://` / check source) would be a single choke point. However, in VS Code webviews, the origin is `vscode-webview://...` and messages from the host are delivered with `event.origin` set. A check could be added. It's a legit security suggestion, but there's risk of false-positives/broken behavior (VS Code versions differ). The file's stated design is "treat data as untrusted" so the defense-in-depth is deliberate. I'd report it as a low-severity maintainability/security note... Hmm. The instructions say to focus on substantive issues and avoid marginal findings. The origin check is a reasonable security hardening given the file itself declares the only legitimate sender is the host. But since the code deliberately validates shape, and the comment acknowledges hostile senders, I think it's worth one comment at low/medium. I'll include it but frame it as defense-in-depth: consider verifying event.origin when running in a webview context, or at minimum document why shape-validation alone is acceptable. Actually, I'd rather focus. Let me weigh: the task checklist includes "Code Security Checks". An origin check is the standard mitigation. I'll include it as low severity with careful wording.

4. `asArray` — `[...value]` copies the array; for a hostile payload, `Array.isArray(value)` with a huge sparse array e.g. `new Array(1e9)`... but the data comes from structured clone of a postMessage — a sparse array with length 2^32-1 can't be cloned (it would throw in structured clone? Actually structured clone preserves holes, so a message with a length-1e9 sparse array... it clones holes efficiently). Then `[...value]` would materialize 1e9 `undefined`s → OOM. That's a plausible DoS from a hostile/compromised frame. Hmm, in webviews, postMessage structured clone of a sparse array of length 1e9: the clone algorithm iterates over own properties, so it's fast, producing a sparse array. Then `[...value]` in asArray iterates all 1e9 indices → hang/OOM. This is a real (if exotic) robustness issue. But the same would apply anywhere iterating. It's a legit performance/DoS note: `value.filter` / spread on untrusted arrays without a length cap. I'd rate low. Also `value.filter` in the item path is safe (filter skips holes but iterates indices... actually filter skips holes entirely and does not call callback, but still iterates the index range O(n)). So a length cap is the mitigation. I think this is worth a low-severity performance/security comment. Hmm — is it too marginal? The file's whole purpose is hardening against untrusted payloads, so bounding array size fits the file's intent. I'll include it as low.

5. Unused exports? `asString` fallback param used. Everything's used.

6. `parseHostMessage` returns `data: {}` for non-record data — this means a handler can't distinguish "no data" from "data was a string". Minor, documented.

7. `postToHost` doesn't catch exceptions from postMessage — a hostile/frozen `window.vscode` getter or a postMessage that throws would propagate. Callers in ExportDialog note "postToHost is synchronous and silently no-ops without the host API". Since the object may be forged (any script on the page can set `window.vscode`), a throwing postMessage would break handlers. Low. Probably skip or merge.

Redirect handling has three problems:
1. The redirect response body is never drained (`response.resume()`/`destroy()`), so the socket stays in the keep-alive pool and leaks — ironic given the comment on the non-200 branch right below.
2. `response.headers.location` may be a relative path or an `http://` URL. `https.get()` throws **synchronously** for both (`ERR_INVALID_URL` / `Protocol "http:" not supported`), and this call happens inside a response callback where the throw is not caught by the Promise executor → uncaught exception in the extension host. A hostile/compromised redirect can therefore kill the host instead of failing the download.
3. No hop counter and no host allow-list → a redirect loop hangs forever, and any origin can be reached (HTTPS→HTTP downgrade).

Resolve the location against the current URL, keep a hop budget, and restrict the protocol/host.

comments.content:
Failure paths leak the write stream and the partial file:
- `response.on("error", reject)` and `fileStream.on("error", reject)` reject without destroying the other side; the fd stays open until GC. On Windows the open handle makes the follow-up `fs.promises.rm(tmp)` fail (EBUSY), so the truncated `.tmp` model survives.
- `fileStream.close()` only closes the fd asynchronously, so the same problem applies to cancellation.
- `signal?.removeEventListener("abort", onAbort)` is only executed on `finish`, leaking a listener on every error path.
Introduce a single `fail(err)` that destroys both sides, removes the abort listener and rejects once.

With `shell: true`, `child` is `/bin/sh -c "command args"`, so `child.kill()` only signals the shell. For anything that is not a single simple command (pipes, `&&`, subshells) the real process and its grandchildren survive, keep running, and keep their stdio/handles open well past the "timed out after Xms" promise resolution — exactly the hang the timeout is meant to prevent. There is also no SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation, so a process ignoring SIGTERM is never actually terminated.

Spawn with `detached: true` and kill the whole process group (falling back to `child.kill()`); note this requires adding `pid` to `ShellChildProcess`.

The timeout message interpolates the raw command and the full joined argv. Callers pipe `result.stderr` straight into user-visible errors (`git-commit-message.ts` builds its `status: "timeout"` message from it), so any token/secret passed as an argument (API key, `--token`, auth header value) is echoed into the UI, logs and issue reports. The same leak exists in the duplicated message in `execFileWithStdinImpl`, and `windowsShellSafetyRejection` likewise embeds the offending raw value in its error text.

Report only the executable name plus the argument count, or redact values that follow credential-ish flags.

`clearTimeout` is wired only to the child's `close` event, so whenever the promise settles without that event the timer stays pending and keeps the Node event loop alive for up to `timeoutMs` (15s by default) — a real problem for the short-lived CLI invocations this module backs, which then appear to "hang" after the work is done. Clear the timer in the settle path instead of relying on `close` (declare `timer` with `let` before the callback, since a stubbed `execFile` may invoke the callback synchronously and would hit a TDZ on a `const`).

`process.env.SHELL` is used unvalidated as the program that will be executed, and `-lc` additionally sources the user's login profile. An environment that a workspace/task/test runner controls (`SHELL=/path/to/attended-binary`) therefore chooses the program that runs, and the value is never validated as an existing shell. Prefer a known-good default, or verify the value against an allowlist (`bash`, `sh`, `zsh`, `fish`) before using it.

Nothing in `src/webview/` registers an `import.meta.hot` dispose hook, and `App.svelte` has no root `onDestroy`. Registering a dispose that unmounts also gives the `app` binding below an actual purpose.

project_summary:
# Pilot / Pi-Agent Extension — Full-Repo Scan Summary

## Top Issues

### 1. The webview ↔ extension-host boundary is trusted end-to-end (security)
The single largest cluster. `src/message-handler.ts` forwards raw `message.data` fields straight into the secret store and global config for `addProvider`, `removeProvider`, `fetchProviderModels`, `setToolConfig`, `setPiUISetting`, `setExtraSkillPaths` — a malformed payload is *persisted*, not just mis-handled. The guard added at the top of `handle()` is defeated by every one of those cases. On the webview side, `src/webview/messages.ts` validates payload *shape* but never `event.origin`/`event.source`, and its array helper has no size bound, so a forged `new Array(4294967295)` passes `Array.isArray`. Same pattern in `ChatPanel.svelte` (destructure throws on `null`; `data.files` assumed array), `SkillsPanel.svelte` (`toSkillInfo` calls `s.name.toLowerCase()` on unvalidated values), `PiPackagesPanel.svelte` (normalizer checks "is array" but not element shape).
**Fix direction:** one shared runtime validator (zod/hand-rolled) at the top of `handle()` that rejects the *entire* message on schema failure, plus `event.source === window` on the webview listener.

### 2. Rendering sinks receive unescaped, attacker-influenceable data
`MessageBubble.svelte` interpolates `edit.lines` and `details.bytes` from the untyped `details?: any` tool payload into `{@html}` **without** `escapeHtml`, while every neighbouring field is escaped — a direct injection hole. Two more in the same file: `renderInline` double-escapes already-escaped substrings (link labels render `&`), and the NUL-sentinel code-block scheme lets a message containing `\u0000CODE0\u0000` substitute a code block into arbitrary positions. `SkeletonLoader.svelte` interpolates `height`/`width` raw into a `style=` attribute (CSS injection: `1px; position: fixed; inset: 0`). `src/session-resources.ts` wraps raw file content in `<file path="...">` with no escaping, so a file containing `</file>` forges the closing boundary of the agent context.
**Fix direction:** escape at the sink, always; add a shared `escapeHtml`-before-`highlightHtml` wrapper; ban unescaped interpolation into `{@html}`.

### 3. Security checks are lexical where the filesystem is not
- `src/session-resources.ts`: the workspace-prefix check passes on a symlink inside the workspace pointing at `/etc/shadow`; the file is read and injected into agent context. Resolve both sides with `fs.realpathSync`.
- `src/loader.cjs`: the pnpm walk-up guard walks the *logical* path with `..`, so a symlink inside the package escapes it and is then handed to `Module._load`.
- `src/git-extension.ts`: case-insensitivity is hardcoded to `win32 || darwin`, wrong in both directions (case-sensitive APFS, `casefold` SMB mounts).

### 4. `src/loader.cjs` — the activation path is the weakest code in the repo
- **Priority is inverted**: the setting-derived path is unshifted first, then the `PATH`-derived path is unshifted *on top*, so `which pi` wins over `pi-agent.binaryPath` — the exact opposite of the documented contract.
- **Unguarded fs**: `fs.readdirSync`/`statSync` calls outside try/catch (EACCES, ELOOP, ENOTDIR) escape `findPiSdkAtPath()` and abort activation.
- **Blocking I/O on the extension host thread**: `which/where pi`, `npm root -g`, `pnpm root -g` are `spawnSync` with 3s timeouts — up to ~9s frozen host before any extension code runs, even when the SDK was already found.
- **Engine mismatch**: the header depends on Node 22+ `require(esm)`, but `engines.vscode: ^1.85.0` is Electron 25 / Node 18 → `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` with only a generic message.
- The stale-closure double-hook guard and the duplicated pnpm scan (~45 lines, copy-pasted) round it out.

### 5. CI and test orchestration can report success on failure
- `scripts/verify.mjs`: `process.exit(code)` truncates to 8 bits — a stage exiting 256 makes the orchestrator exit 0. This is exactly the "never exit 0 on failure" contract the file header claims.
- `scripts/run-node-tests.mjs`: the suite *appends* its summary to the previous run's report and this script never clears it, so a **stale report decides this run's exit code** — false green.
- `src/test/runTest.ts`: `isGreenReport` accepts reports that also contain `UNCAUGHT`/`UNHANDLED` markers; the report file is not isolated per run.
- `scripts/run-webview-tests.mjs`: hardcoded spec list — a newly added `src/test/webview/*.test.mjs` is silently never executed (green forever).
- `run-clean.mjs`: the env scrubber blocks the `VSCODE_` prefix and runs *before* discovery, so any user/CI-supplied `VSCODE_PATH` is deleted; the "newest" version sort is a plain `String` sort (`1.10.0 < 1.9.0`); only the Linux `bin/code` layout is resolved; `accessSync` defaults to `F_OK` so a directory passes as an executable.
- `package.json`: the E2E `test` script embeds POSIX `if … then … fi`, so `pnpm test` fails immediately on Windows.

### 6. Blocking child processes and sync FS on the shared extension-host thread
`src/utils/native-addons.ts` runs `spawnSync` for `prebuild-install` (30s) and `node-gyp` (300s) *per copy* from the activation path — a multi-minute frozen extension host. Also `footer-manager.ts` `resolveGitBranch` (2 fs round-trips per ancestor, every tick), `pi-binary.ts` manifest reads (2N syscalls from a `.map`), `git-extension.ts` `realpathSync.native` inside an `async` function, `session-resources.ts` an `async` function that is entirely `existsSync`/`statSync`/`readFileSync`, and `src/loader.cjs` above. **This is the single best performance lever in the codebase.**

### 7. Duplicated constants and config that have already drifted
Every one of these is a real, observable divergence, not a hypothetical:
- `pi-agent.*` → provider-options mapping duplicated between `extension.ts` `activate()` and the config listener.
- `runes: true` in `svelte.config.js` **and** hardcoded in `scripts/webview-test-loader.mjs` — the webview test run stops reflecting what Vite compiles.
- `DEFAULT_VSCODE_VERSION = "1.85.0"` in `scripts/dl-vscode.mjs` has no link to `engines.vscode: "^1.85.0"`.
- `THINKING_LEVELS` duplicated in `SettingsPanel.svelte`; the same `~/.pi/agent/npm/node_modules/better-sqlite3` literal appears twice in `native-addons.ts`.
- `SessionItem` is declared three times (`webview/types/index.ts`, `src/session-manager.ts:19`, `SessionTree.svelte:6`); the image payload type is re-declared inline in 5+ host files; `OpenConfigFileKey` is a hand-written mirror of `src/protocol/types.ts:28` mirrored again by `OPEN_CONFIG_FILES`.
- `getVsCodeApi` is byte-identical in `PiPackagesPanel`, `SettingsPanel`, `SkillsPanel` — and the `app.d.ts` declaration models it as freely re-callable, which is false (second call throws).
- `update-checker.ts`: ~80 lines of details-building and dialog flow duplicated between two paths, already drifted (one shows `pkg.packageName`).

### 8. Floating promises and unhandled rejections
`src/extension-ui-context.ts` `custom()` returns a promise that **can never settle** if the factory doesn't call `done()` — no timeout, no abort. `update-checker.ts` chains a second dialog and returns early; `binary-service.ts` and `loader.cjs` discard `showErrorMessage` returns; `message-handler.ts` has `void promise` with no catch; `extension.ts` command handlers `await` `newSession()`/`switchSession()` with no try/catch. `src/utils/shell.ts`'s `clearTimeout` is wired only to `close`, so the 15s timer keeps the event loop alive on every settled-without-close path.

### 9. Webview accessibility is systematically incomplete
`src/webview/styles/global.css`: `--color-border` is ~1.9:1 against the background *and* is the only boundary for default buttons; no `color-scheme: dark`; `:active` transforms clip against `overflow: hidden`; the reduced-motion block misses `animation`/`scroll-behavior`; focus rings are defeated by scoped `outline: none` at higher specificity. Component-side: `Header.svelte` dropdowns have no Escape and no `aria-expanded`, `role="button"` handles Enter but not Space; `OnboardingTour.svelte` has `aria-modal="true"` dialogs with **no focus trap and no focus restore**, and only stops propagation for `Escape` so app-level hotkeys still mutate the app behind the overlay; `SettingsPanel.svelte`'s toggle has no accessible name; `VoiceCapture.svelte` flips the accessible name *and* `aria-pressed` together; `Toast.svelte`'s `role="alert"` names only the title so the message is never announced.

### 10. Repo hygiene / config debt that already produces wrong behaviour
`tsconfig.json` carries an unused `DOM` lib, dead `declaration` output, a dead `@/*` alias, a redundant `baseUrl` and an `ignoreDeprecations` escape hatch that exists only because of that `baseUrl`. `.lintstagedrc.json` omits `js`, so `svelte.config.js` is skipped by prettier and eslint at commit time. `.prettierignore` ignores source-controlled files (`pnpm-workspace.yaml` with its security overrides, `patches/`, `media/voice/README.md`). `.gitignore` blanket-ignores `src/**/*.js` and all of `.vscode/`, and `.env.*` swallows `.env.example`. `fallow-baselines/health.json` references two paths (`src/extension.ts`, `src/test/mocks/vscode-shim.ts`) that are not keys in `finding_counts`. `LICENSE` has a corrupted duplicated block. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` uses a **third-party action by mutable tag** (`pnpm/action-setup@v4`) and runs PR-controlled code with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` persisted in `.git/config`.
